utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 17th of June, 2008. Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel and the OTP representatives and all the people helping us including the interpreters. Mr. Registrar, you have a few IT numbers for us don't you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The OTP has submitted its response to documents tendered by 1D and 3D through witness 1D AA the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 00807 and IC 00808 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed for you to continue with the examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom, good afternoon, sir. If I could get the usher to lower the ELMO. It's direct in my line of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now the next couple of documents deal with the friendship and cooperation agreement so if I could direct your attention to 1D 01942, that would be in binder 1, Your Honours. Now, what I'm showing you sir dated 17 July 1992, it's from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This would have been a session the 145th Session. Do you recall whether you were present?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't get any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see when we turn to the first page or number two, we see that you are listed there as the Secretary-General. If we then -- as I understand it, it was during this session where there was a discussion concerning the forming of a delegation to go to the Republic of Croatia and we see that as part of item 1 on page 3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see that the delegation was going to be for the Presidency or for BiH it was going to be Izetbegovic, Ljubic and Mr. Pelivan. So we had somebody from the Presidency, somebody from the assembly, and somebody from the government. If we now go back to page number 2 under agenda we see section of a delegation for the visit of the Republic of Croatia and platform for talks. Do you see where it says "platform" sir? Under agenda, number one?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01773. We see -- this is in binder 1. We don't see a date, but it's titled "Platform for regulating the relationship with the Republic of Croatia." Do you know, sir, whether, in fact this is the platform is being discussed in the minutes of the meeting of 17 July 1992. Take a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we focus on item number one, it says, "Cooperation in the military and international field with the aim of defending Bosnia and Herzegovina from aggressors." Who are the aggressors at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the definition of the BH Presidency, it was the then already former JNA, the Republic of Serbia, the republics of Serbia Montenegro, the FRY and forces from within Bosnia and Herzegovina led by the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, unless there are any questions from the Bench, I will move on to the next segment. Very well. Okay. Let's turn our attention now, this is with respect to Dr. Jadranko Prlic and let's look at document 1D 02014. This is in binder 1, Your Honours. 1D 02014. This is dated 5 October 1992 and I -- the subject matter is "Request for a share in the commodity loan provided by Turkey." And here Dr. Jadranko Prlic is president of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, is writing to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning a loan which would appear to be in the amount of 50 million American dollars from Turkey. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in fact, there was a loan from Turkey for that amount or to any other amount?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain but I think there was a loan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 02685. Binder 3, Your Honours. I apologise for having to shuffle back and forth. 1D 02685. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you see that it's signed by the deputy prime minister that was the gentleman you spoke of yesterday who was killed in the UN armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. He was the deputy prime minister. I think that's what his position was called officially, Hakija Turajlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we saw Dr. Prlic's letter which was 5 October 1992 in the previous document which was 1D 02014 and here in 1D 02685, on 17 October 1992 we have this gentleman indicating that: "We have considered carefully your request of 5 October which we received under number 29-22/S 92 referring to using a Turkish loan of US $50 million." It goes on to say, "We hereby inform that you this loan has still not been approved in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However talks with Turkish official authorities about this matter have been scheduled for the near future, of which you will be promptly informed." "We also wish to confirm the RBH government's firm decision to use part of this loan, should it be approved, to cover the needs of the armed conflict also in this area." From this document, can we draw any conclusions, sir, concerning the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its relationship towards the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can certainly draw a conclusion. Firstly, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to slow down -- Mr. Akmadzic, none of that was translated because you're speaking way too fast. So you need to please slow down. I kindly -- I beg you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can draw the following conclusion from this: The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised the Croatian Defence Council. We can also draw another conclusion. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was willing to grant financial assistance to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we look at the next -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to clarify one issue with the witness, if possible. It is a bit interesting to note that the very paragraph which you kindly quoted, Mr. Karnavas, here we read that "We hereby inform you that this loan has still not been approved in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." and it was also mentioned in the original letter that [B/C/S spoken]. I'm not quite sure as far as this loan is concerned did it need approval by the government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina because in a way, in Dr. Prlic's letter, it is being referred to as a credit -- I mean as a loan to be transmitted to the government from and by Turkey. So then I would like to ask the witness what was the legal issue here involved that the loan had to be approved by the government concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I wasn't prime minister. However, based on what I know, the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina asked for a loan. Was Turkey to grant that loan request, was the money to be received by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government decision would have been to allocate part of that money to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sorry, but following up on Judge Prandler's question, I'd like to ask you this: I have the two letters in front of me. In Dr. Prlic's letter, it is in English, but I'm trying to translate that into French, he's asking that the Croatian Defence Council receive or get a share of the loan by way of a third of it. That's the letter by Dr. Prlic of the 5th of October, 1992. In the response by Hakija Turajlic on the 17th of October 1992, in that very last paragraph precisely, he said this: The loan should also be used to cover the needs of the armed conflict in this area. As far as I can see, it's not very clear, is it? You could interpret any which way. The answer does not say that the loan would be given to the HVO but part of it, at least, will be used for the armed conflict but who is going to get the money? That's not said in this paragraph, is it? What do you think of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even before this letter as well as after it, there was an agreement that was not specified or written down anywhere to the effect that all the means would be distributed to all three parties in equal shares, 30 per cent, roughly speaking. Or there would be two 50 per cent cuts as long as there were only two parties involved. I said yesterday that the three parties were the Serb party, the Muslim party, and the Croat party. In this specific conflict at this specific time, the two parties involved were the Croat and the Muslim. I would like to provide an additional explanation. This is a loan in goods, it is merely expressed here in monetary terms. This could potentially have comprised both money and goods or either one of those simply because it's not specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have a question, Judge Trechsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your last answer is in a way a non-answer because you start off saying "This was a loan in goods ..." and then you continue saying," ... but it could also have comprised both money and goods or either of one of those." So what you are saying -- first you say it was in goods and not in money and in the end, you say it could also have been entirely in money. Maybe you do not know more specifically, that is quite possible and I would not blame you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can tell from this letter and the reply by Mr. Hakija Turajlic, the loan had not yet been approved. It could, for example, have been $10 million in money or 40 million -- and 40 million in goods, goods that would have been used for the purposes of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and for the benefit of the population. As I said, I wasn't prime minister at the time this was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So in fact, Witness, this is more or less speculation, you do not know what it would have been, it had not been to your own knowledge at that time specified what it would be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, that had not been specified yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question because we could devote hours to this issue, but I will go straight away to the core of the matter. When you said it was not approved, did the loan have to be approved by the government or by the parliamentary assembly in as it was a loan and therefore it could have repercussions on the financial balance of the financial bill which normally was to be adopted year by year, so I guess that there would be changes or additions so that has to be endorsed by parliament. Is that why you said that it had to be approved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we are looking at here is 1992 which can be seen as breaking down into two distinct parts. The first part, the war had not been underway properly and the other part, and this was about the war budget. In the first part, the budget was a regular one based on what I know and I'm saying again I wasn't prime minister at the time, these are amounts that were approved by decisions during the war meaning there were two parties involved, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the one hand, and the Republic of Turkey on the other. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina applied for this loan but by this time, it had not yet received one from Turkey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd like to point out that on 1D 02014 Dr. Jadranko Prlic's letter it quite clearly states in English "Commodity loan of $50 million" a commodity loan which is why the gentleman answered the way he did. Also I should point out that the purpose of us showing this letter was not so much whether the loan was granted or not but rather to establish that the government of BiH recognised the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That was the real essence of introducing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document now sir, 1D 00898, binder 1. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we see at the bottom, we see first of all it's 17 November 1992, Sarajevo. We see your name president of the government, so by November 17, I take it you were president of the government of RBiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for about a week by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, we have a decision by you -- by the government, you signing it on behalf of the government as the president of it, to appoint and authorize Dr. Jadranko Prlic the president of the Croatian Defence Council to represent the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and you go on that he's hereby being appointed a member of the RBiH staff for collection of the items to help the RBiH population to survive. Sir, was this a collective decision or was this your decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an official decision of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was this published in the Official Gazette so everyone could see that this decision had indeed been issued by the government of RBiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and the entire procedure was implemented that this decision required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, based on that answer let's look at 1D 02147, 1D 02147. Your Honours, I believe that would be right after the previous -- that would be in binder 1. Do you have this, sir? Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And here we see the November 20th, 1992. At the bottom, we see your name, again president of the government and here it says "Powers" and this -- what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to a decision of the BH government that we mentioned a while ago, Dr. Prlic received this letter of authorisation. He was going about his work and this is something that he had been allowed to do by the government and he was to show this document to any appropriate bodies who would then allow him to get on with his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if I understanding it correctly, you have the decision that was taken and published and this an implementing instrument, a power of attorney that then allows Dr. Jadranko Prlic to act on behalf of the decision that has already been reached, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could take this decision and work both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and wherever the logistics centres happened to be, which for the most part was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we don't see a signature in the Croatian version. I'm sure at least one of the Judges will probably be asking themselves why there is no signature there and how can this be a valid power of attorney and one to be acted upon if there is no signature by the president of the government. Do you have an explanation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was issued by the government's administrative unit. It was valid as long as one attached the government -- the appropriate government decision with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could now then go on to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you may be going exactly where I'm looking for, namely, we read in the last one paragraph that "these powers shall become effective on the day when they are granted." Now, the question was were they ever and on what day were they granted? I thought that might be your next document because I have not seen them all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I said the other day -- last week, I believe, that great minds think alike. I'm speaking about your mind of course not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have my doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if we could have an answer from the gentleman concerning that question.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discrepancy is three days in terms of the dates this document took effect as soon as it had been adopted, this last document not the previous one. This takes effect on the 20th of November, 1992, this letter of authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, I'm not quite convinced. The decision that we had previously was taken on the 17th of November and this is three days later but the sentence I referred to refers to the future " ... shall become effective on the day when they were granted." So that cannot easily be three days ago. Otherwise he would have said "... have become effective on the day the decision was taken."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I can remember quite well that my lawyers had told me that it would be good for Mr. Prlic to have this kind of letter of authorisation in addition to the decision. It was my opinion that the decision would suffice. They did it the way they did it. Dr. Prlic could not use the letter of authorisation before he received it. That's simple logic. It is possible that he might have used only the government decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Might I ask the interpreters to read the sentence in question in -- well, to translate it? Maybe someone could read them. I could not, I'm afraid. Perhaps the witness, could you read the last but one paragraph? "Ovlascenje" is the first word, I suppose, so the translators could give it to us in English. Maybe there is a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it. "This letter of authorisation shall take effect on the day when it is adopted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll leave it at that. I remain perplexed, I must tell you. I'm sure your lawyer then was not Mr. Karnavas but someone of a lesser quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It could be also stylistic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if you allow me, I would like to put two questions to you. This document is very important, I think. Therefore, we should focus on its meaning. Here's a document from the government, the date is the 20th of November, 1992. Upon reading this document, we see that Dr. Prlic, who is the president of the Croatian Defence Council is given an assignment. He's supposed to represent the government Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Therefore, this document has legal repercussions. Indeed, Dr. Prlic is supposed to represent the government with all that it entails. According to your knowledge -- well, have you spoken about it to Mr. Izetbegovic because this document, for a lawyer, means that you acknowledge explicitly the role played by the Croatian Defence Council in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So did you tell Mr. Izetbegovic about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were three key institutions in the state: The assembly, the Presidency, and the government. And those three institutions had their powers in accordance with the constitution. This decision on this kind of representation pertains to the government, not the Presidency. It is based on the previous recognition of the Croatian Defence Council. I did inform President Izetbegovic about that, but I did not table this at the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have to say here -- but this is something that I'm not sure about -- that in this regard, President Izetbegovic told me, or perhaps it was at that time that 1 million German marks had been transferred to the Croatian Defence Council by way of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have another question to put to you. A while ago you said that these powers shall become effective on the day when they are granted. We are therefore under the impression that this document was supposed to be published officially. That was mentioned by the lawyer. Therefore, was this document ever published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or was it never published? That's what I would like to say -- to know, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that but I can confirm that the decision itself was published. I'm not a lawyer and I cannot really see any substantial difference between the two documents, and I think, it is my belief that the first document was the basic document and it was published in the Official Gazette and that in and of itself, it could be effective, but I may not be right in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is a document published in the Official Gazette about the HVO, there are consequences from a legal standpoint, that means that you somehow acknowledge the existence of this entity. The government or the president acknowledges the existence of that entity. If there is no publication, it means that there is a de facto entity, but if there is an official document mentioning the HVO and indicating that the HVO is playing a role in the Republic, a lawyer is entitled to assume that this entity is acknowledged by the government in power. But you said that you couldn't give any answer about this document which is 1D 02147. But you said that another document was published.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other document, the basic document was published and it contains -- it is couched in the same terms as this document here, the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this basic document, maybe Mr. Karnavas has it, but I do not have it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the gentleman -- I may be mistaken is speaking about 1D 00898 which is the decision, if we look at the very last line, it says, "This decision shall be published in the Official Gazette of RBiH." So -- and having worked there I know that it takes sometime from the moment a decision is made until the actual official publication because it comes out on a monthly basis, but I don't know what the procedure was back then but this is what this document says now whether it was indeed published or not, we -- it is our understanding what we are presenting you is from the Official Gazette, that is the decision 1D 00898 is actually a copy from the Official Gazette that was published at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 01945. This is in binder 1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, this is a -- if we look at this, you see that it is signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. It is dated 12 December 1992 and it's titled "Protest" or that's the subject matter. We see at the very -- sir, the very next document. There's no need for you to read -- going through the entire binder it's just the very next document, 1D 01945. Okay. All right. Good. Now, if we look at the very first paragraph, we can see your name there it says, I'll just read part of it -- I'll read the paragraph: "The immediate cause of our address to the Presidency and the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the document of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, but the underlying reasons are diverse and do not" it says in English "do not knew" they are not known, apparently is what it says in B/C/S. "We urge you, Mr. Akmadzic, to have the government and Presidency discuss this protest of ours and to have this two high-ranking bodies of the BH state respond to it in clear terms." Now, in the second paragraph, we see Dr. Jadranko Prlic stating toward the middle of it: "We are as unrelenting in favour of preserving the BH statehood as we are committed to the idea that the state in its internal organisation must match the interests of the Croat people residing within it. In this respect, we genuinely accept the solutions for the internal organisation of the BH offered by the European Community namely for a BH as a compound state community of three constitutive peoples, Croats Muslims Serbs composed of three constitutive units formed and organised on the basis of the already accepted principles from ethnic to sacral ones." Anyway, if we go on to the next page, there seems to be a complaint that Halilovic is making certain statements and it actually starts from the bottom of the previous page, Your Honours, last part of the paragraph, it says: "There were talks held along those lines on several occasions about cooperation between HVO units and BH army about the status of the areas which had been defended or liberated, about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO as a form of provisional executive authority in the region until such time as a final solution was found. We received assurances that the official bodies of the BH government and Presidency accepted and acknowledged the actual state of affairs, the role and the contribution of the Croat people in defending the home land. However, almost as a rule in the aftermath of such talks and accords high-ranking officials from top political state or military leadership always publicly refute these agreements and planned cooperation. We can no longer be regarded or treated as happenstance but rather unfortunately as duplicitous political activity which directly works to the detriment of the BH as a state, its survival and the interests of the Croat and Muslim peoples." Sir, do you recall receiving this protest letter from Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, what was at the bottom of this complaint? I mean in the very first paragraph he mentions Sefer Halilovic who was, at the time, the head of the ABiH army and also the founder of the Patriotic League when it was secretly founded, we know that. But do you know what exactly Dr. Jadranko Prlic was complaining about?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I did submit this document to the Presidency too. That it was considered by the Presidency but no specific conclusions were made. Dr. Prlic is here protesting on behalf of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina against its treatment which is perceived to be unfair and he's also protesting against the use of the term "so-called Croatian Defence Council" by Mr. Halilovic whereas the Bosnian authorities had already accepted the Croatian Defence Council as a constituent element of the armed forces. Dr. Prlic goes on to say that international negotiations have to be accepted as do the plans for the restructuring of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and cooperation between the two segments of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the next document, 1D 02663. 1D 02663. That's in binder 2, Your Honours. This is the 182nd Session of the Presidency held on December 26th, 1992. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know exactly in which page in the B/C/S version, but if we look at -- in the English version at the top of the page, Your Honours, it would be 01806416. That's the ERN number. 6416 if you just look at the first four digits, that would be sufficient. Do you have that, sir? Perhaps you may want to follow the English version, it might be -- usher, could we have your assistance?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 6416 are the last four digits, and we would kindly ask the usher to assist us as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We see over here your name Mile Akmadzic and you say: "I would say that it would be good if Mr. Jadranko Prlic on behalf of the Croatian Defence Council and Herceg-Bosna sent a letter to the government and the Presidency, we have put it on the agenda of the government as Mr. Sefer was absent." Then you go on. So I don't want to go into exactly what transpired because we can read it all for ourselves and you did indicate that nothing happened, no resolution occurred, but is this what you were telling us earlier? That you brought this matter to the attention of the Presidency? Was it at this session?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see, if we turn a couple of pages, we see Mr. Halilovic's name, and can we assume that Mr. Halilovic was present at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as an aside, there's another issue that might be worth noting because there is this issue that has been -- that is part of the indictment known as the "Croatisation" and one of the elements is the use of the Croatian language. Now, if I could direct your attention to the pages 01806433, the last four digits are 6433. Let me -- just look at the top right hand -- okay. Now, let me just ask -- we're going to be talking -- I'm going to focus your attention on this Mr. Campara but before that, let me ask a question. Do you recall whether it was at this session that the issue of language came up?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the issue of language was raised at this session, and I did take part in the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we know yesterday -- from yesterday that you graduated from the Sarajevo University in languages, English, German, Latin, so I assume that you were fully aware of -- fully conversant in Bosnian-Herzegovinian languages, whatever languages were used at the time, could you please tell us was there a language called Bosnian or Bosniak at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the official usage was the following -- or rather the official language was Croatian or Serbian and the people generally abbreviated that and this was general practice in schools, too, to Serbo-Croatian and -- or Croato-Serbian. The Bosnian language did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look and see what was going on at the Presidency session where Izetbegovic was present on this particular occasion, and again we're talking about December 26th, 1992. We have Mr. Campara who says: "Article 4 says in the republic of BiH, the officially used language is Serbo-Croatian or Croat-Serbian language with Ijekavian speech. He then goes on to say: "And we same to the opinion that such formulation can no longer be there especially because there is no Bosnian language there et cetera and the openly possibility will be and the Presidency can give the initiative now and based on this that the matter should go to the commission for constitutional matters so that this provision is made void for the period during the war and until a new constitution is passed. Then this provision will no longer exist, and the language of all nations will be in use." At which point further down, you say, "Which language will we be speaking by then?" Campara says: "Then you will speak Serbo-Croatian, Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian. The decree will say the President Izetbegovic in the meantime, we must be silent a bit." And I take it that was a joke. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Ganic says, "They say that we should add -- we should just as Bosnian among the other -- these permanent combinations. Campara: "We cannot do that."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Pejanovic: "We will speak as we speak, and we will probably call our language Bosnian language and other languages as required by the nations that live here. As this really is not an urgent matter, it should be concluded that that will be solved in the regular procedure of passing a new constitution, which I hope will be passed soon." Then you say: "I agree that we should do that. However, it will be difficult to give the language a name. First of all, the language used by Vuk Karadzic and Ljudevit Gaj, who were creators of the Croatian and Serbian languages is Herzegovinian." That should be clear and of course there is some laughter there. Campara further down says, "Mr. President, I propose that you should give initiative to the assembly commission for constitutional matters to consider this request." And here is what Alija Izetbegovic says at the time who is also president of the SDA, head of the largest Muslim party in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslim representatives of the peace talks: "This is not a bad proposal, so that people cannot say that we did not react. Let us say that this should be given to the commission for constitutional matters of the assembly. As Churchill said: 'If you want that an issue is never solved without anybody's responsibility, give it to some commission.' Very well, it is all right. I think this is a proposal. Let the commission consider it. Therefore, the matter has been sent to the commission for constitutional matters." Sir, you were present when this discussion took place. Why was it necessary to have this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a debate about language. I think you left out what Mr. Pejanovic said, that's in line 3 on this page. When I said that this language was actually the language from Herzegovina, and Mr. Pejanovic said, "It is still best preserved there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that Vuk Karadzic, the father of the Serbian language and Ljudevit Gaj, the father of the Croatian language if we can put it that way and we can in a sense, in mid-19th century took language spoken in Herzegovina as the basis for the Croatian and the Serbian language and also language in eastern Bosnia as it was spoken there, and that at that time, Croatian writers and Vuk Karadzic himself used the Ekavian variant as indicated here; and this whole debate is actually about what the language in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be called, given that it was now an independent sovereign state with three constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next page this is what you say and I think this might be relevant to this whole discussion. Akmadzic: "One thing should be borne in mind that every nation has the right to give its language its own name. And then the question is can it be called after something else. In any case, every nation that speaks a certain language has a right to give it its own name. Austrians and Americans have never exercised that right." Then we hear from Izetbegovic: "One can call his language whatever he wants. We should not ban that. We will probably say that one can call the language we speak whatever he wants: Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian. Let them call it whatever they want. Of course, there are other repercussions here. It needs to be stated in graduation certificates which language it is, a mother tongue. Very well. This issue is forwarded to the commission." Now, from this exchange and from what Izetbegovic is saying, can you draw any conclusions as far as making distinctions between the languages people are speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were three constituent peoples, and they all spoke as they liked. At this time, the language was called Serbian or Croatian, Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. The third people had not yet decided what they would call theirs. Now, they are voicing an ambition for a third segment to be added to this one language, the Bosnian segment making it effectively a total of three languages. We Croats were always advocating equal rights for all the groups in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Are we talking about an entirely different language with different grammar, different pronunciations, different vocabulary or as the saying goes, a rose is a rose by any other name?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are looking at three varieties of the same language, if you like. Everybody understands everybody else. Nevertheless, each of the peoples had the right to call their language whatever they liked. That is why back in Washington, we provided for the right for the Muslims to call themselves Bosniaks. Each of the peoples had the right to call their language whatever they liked. That was why back in Washington, we had agreed that the Bosniaks would be allowed to call their language Bosnian or Bosniak. Bosniak as opposed to Bosnian, and Bosnian is the term being used frequently here because Bosnian is all the three groups -- all the three groups were Bosnians, plus people from Herzegovina, the Herzegovinians. As for the Muslims, we made it possible for them to refer to their people as Bosniak as well as the language, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document and we'll go back to what we were earlier discussing before we went off on that little frolic. 1D 02077, this is the next document in your binder, this would be in binder 1 and this is dated 9 October 1992. This is from "Oslobodjenje." Where is this publication published?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is published in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It says here the subject "Izetbegovic's press conference in Mostar and his views of the Muslim-Croatian relations." I'm not going to read the entire article but just focus your attention on the last two paragraphs of page 1, it says: "He also announced that soon members of a coordination committee would be appointed to coordinate military operations between Croatia and BH against the joint Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor. Members have already been appointed by the Croatian side and the BH side has agreed that two representatives of the BH army and one HVO representative should be appointed from their side. The HVO will appoint its representative in a day or two to the BH army will immediately follow suit." Now, here we're talking about relations between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is being discussed here is relations between the Croat people and the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The segment that I read -- just follow me?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Step by step, we'll get there. What I read, this is -- we're talking about Croatia and BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and their relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now we go to the next one, next paragraph: "Izetbegovic stated that soon a single command of the armed forces of BH would be established consisting of the leaders of the BH army and the HVO. The president of the BH Presidency described the establishment of the Council of Muslims of Herzegovina as an understandable reaction to what the Croatian side had done, but an unacceptable path towards the resolution of the problems of BH and an unacceptable path for the Muslims in BH to take." So, it seems from this aspect what conclusion can we draw? Because he talks about a single command of the armed forces and then he talks about BH army and HVO.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he's talking about here is also the relations between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and within Bosnia and Herzegovina, he's talking about the relations between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council which together make up the armed forces of BH. He's talking about cooperation, about appointments to these two segments of the armed forces of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the very last paragraph, it says: "Yesterday, Alija Izetbegovic held talked with the president of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna Dr. Jadranko Prlic, prime minister of the war government of Mostar, Jadranko Topic, and so on and so forth. And if we look at the photograph in the picture, this is the original version. I know it's kind of tough to look at but you recognise the faces. Do you see who is along with Mr. Izetbegovic, can you recognise that individual? Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: We don't have the photograph. At least I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the Croatian -- the B/C/S version. I can lead the witness, Your Honour. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. That was when he had more hair, I think. Okay. If we could go on to the -- we're all going south in that direction, some sooner than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go on to the next topic. This deals with logistics centres. Yesterday you indicated that logistics centres had been set up and I very quickly want to go through some documents with you to establish that. If we could look at 1D 01145, all of these documents, Your Honours, are in binder 5 -- binder 1. Here we see a decision to appoint the director of the logistics centre in Ploce and this is Mr. Raguz; correct? Correct? And he's a Croat as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next one, 1D 01146. This is for Rijeka, Stjepan Meler and he's also a Croat, at least it looks like it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The next is 1D 01147, this is for Split, a Munib Karavdic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karavdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the next one is 1D 01403. This is to appoint an acting head of the department for economic affairs and humanitarian aid at the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia and this would be a Dr. Josip Goluza and I think that was the gentleman we saw the letter from yesterday, the protest?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Josip Goluza, a Croat. He was government's office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And speaking of that very quickly, if you could inform us when you say the government's office in Zagreb, could you please explain what that office was all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war first began, as soon as April 1992, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina first reached an agreement that internationally and for diplomatic purposes, they would be aiding one another. Bosnia and Herzegovina proceeded to set up an office in Zagreb, rather the BH government did. The office continued to operate until the BH embassy was first established in Zagreb. Likewise, Croatia set up an embassy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll go on to the next document, 1D 01287. This is a decision to appoint a director for the logistics centre in Ploce and here we see a Salko Handzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the next decision is 1D 01301 where we see -- this is a decision dismissing Mr. Raguz, the one that we saw earlier on; correct? This is April 29, 1993 now.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at 1D 02292, 1D 02292, and of course it will not fail to escape the attention of the Judges that we not see a seal or signature here, but we do see that this is a summary, at least what it's translated, it says this is a summary of deliveries to the army of BH and the Croatian Defence Council as per requests of the Ministry of Defence of the republic of BH in the Main Staff of the armed forces and it's the Visoko logistics centre. Now, do you know anything about this document? Can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can confirm is that there was a logistics centre in Visoko, the distance between Visoko and Sarajevo being about 40 kilometres. This centre provided supplies mostly for the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document 1D 01282, this is a decision to establish logistics centres to provide supplies to the inhabitants of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and we see Visoko. Of course, if we see the date on this is 10 May whereas the previous document was 25 January 1993. My question is: Is this a different logistics centre or do centres exist -- were there two types, one for armaments and another one for supplies, if you know, supplies for inhabitants, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first centre that we mentioned in Visoko was a military logistics centre. The others were for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last document in this -- for this topic and that's 1D 01302. We see this is a decision to establish the logistics centre for humanitarian aid in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And this is 29 April 1993. Do you know why it might have been necessary to -- or why it was necessary to establish a logistics centre for humanitarian aid in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, most of the shared border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, about three-thirds [as interpreted] in fact, throughout the war and in peacetime, Bosnia and Herzegovina was getting most of its supplies from Croatia. It is for this reason that logistics centres were set up in Croatia's principal ports but not only there. It is from there that humanitarian aid and other kinds of aid was arriving to Bosnia and Herzegovina for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go into another topic that's going to take much longer than say ten minutes so perhaps -- oh, good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. We have just reviewed a series of decisions. In each of them, for instance, we don't need to look at them, no need to repeat them but in each of them, it is said that the decision will enter into effect when it is published in the Official Gazette. I'd like to know one thing: Can the witness confirm that in this time of conflict, the Official Gazette was still being published and that the said decisions were indeed promulgated further to the law, in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These decisions were published in keeping with the law that applied at the time. The Official Gazette was published in a minimal form. Some of the decisions took immediate effect. These particular ones took effect as soon as they were published in the Official Gazette. The decisions that, for reasons of time, or because of the need for an urgent implementation could not be published in the Official Gazette took immediate effect. Sometimes some decisions were meant to be published at a later stage in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's best to have a break now, then you can start with a new topic. 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The next topic we're going to talk about, Mr. Akmadzic, deals with the issue of districts, the "okrug." So if you could look at 1D 00509, binder 1 for Your Honours. Do you have it, sir? Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is a -- it says it's 13 August 1992 and it's a decree with the power of law on establishment of work and work of districts. Were you familiar with this decree back then?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please explain a little bit to the Trial Chamber, so we can have an understanding, of what this decree is about?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of August, 1992 is a time when the war was in full swing and Sarajevo was entirely encircled. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was based in Sarajevo, wasn't able to keep in touch on a permanent basis with the local authorities throughout the republic. For this reason, the BH Presidency, acting as an assembly, adopted a decision -- or rather passed a decree to establish a number of districts, a total of ten, I believe, including the city of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were a member -- were you a member of this Presidency or War Presidency, I guess by this point. Were you a member of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the Secretary-General at the time, I wasn't a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you have an opinion whether this is a -- this decree, whether it's within the constitution of the then RBiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency Bosnia and Herzegovina deemed that it was necessary to set up these districts although it was by no means certain that this was a constitutional move because the constitution did not provide for the establishment of such districts. Any amendments -- no amendments to the constitution can be introduced by either the Presidency or the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 8, that might help us a little bit because here, it talks about the rights and duties of the district. Were these functions that are under Article 8, were these the functions of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not the functions of the municipalities and even previously, especially when it came to mobilisation, municipalities were involved but only as far as they cooperated with the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at -- let's leave this decree for now and let look at the next document 1D 02418, 1D 02418. That's binder number 2, Your Honours. We saw that the decree was passed on 13 August 1992. This is now a letter dated 31 January 1993 and it's signed by Izetbegovic for the BH SDA. So it would appear that Mr. Izetbegovic is sending this on behalf of his party and it says at the top, "In accordance with the principles of the constitutional and legal order of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind reading slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "In accordance with the principles of the constitutional and legal order of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted in Geneva, and the Charter of Muslims of Herzegovina and on behalf of PH SDA, I hereby fully" I underscore that "fully authorise the president of the SDA regional board for Herzegovina Mr. Zijad Damirovic, leader of the team of experts to be sent -- to be set up -- by the SDA regional board for Herzegovina to start constituting the proposed province of Mostar in cooperation with the representatives of the Croatian people and to finalise this task in terms of constitutional, legal, political personnel and functional completion of Mostar province." The last paragraph says, "In keeping with this authorisation, the president of the SDA regional board for Herzegovina and the board itself are obliged to ensure democratic unity of the SDA in Herzegovina in the performance of this task." So here we are several months after the passage of the decree, Izetbegovic now is sending this authorisation for the province of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my question is: Is there some contradiction between the decree which was supposed to establish these districts setting aside the issue of whether this was constitutional or not and this authorisation to his party to cooperate with the Croats in the establishment of the province of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the president, Mr. Izetbegovic, here is not distinguishing between the role of the president of the Presidency and the president of the Party for Democratic Action. He, in his capacity as party president, has certain powers but he doesn't have in his capacity as party president such powers as belong to state bodies. There is another thing that I would like to point out in this context. The 31st of January, 1993. This is a time after the Geneva talks on the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In a way, President Izetbegovic is trying to remain in keeping with the instructions that were issued in Geneva and this had to do with the establishment of the provinces. In a way, he is seeking cooperation with the Croats. I suppose that also means the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the original version, we see that there is a signature. Can you tell us to any degree of certainty whether, in fact, this is Mr. Izetbegovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that, and I can be completely sure about it because I know his signature well, and I know him well. This is Mr. Izetbegovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well let look and see what happens a month or so later. 1D 02565, 1D 02565. And that's in binder number 2, Your Honour. Here we have a letter dated March 3, 1993. It's addressed to Mr. Demirovic from a Professor Dr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, and, of course, attached to it we see that there is a letter to Mr. Pasalic who is the commander of the 4th Corps of the ABiH and at the bottom we also see that this is supposed to be copied to Dr. Jadranko Prlic which we also see on the very first page. "Please forward attached materials to Mr. Prlic after you make copies of all materials for your use." Now, if we look at page number 2 to Pasalic, it says here, and this is from the vice-president of the government sending a letter to the commander of the army of BiH, he says: "We are sending you the conclusion of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the urgent implementation of activities with the aim of setting up of Mostar and Livno districts." Now let's just stop there. Is this in keeping the Mostar Livno districts, is this in keeping with the previous document that we saw signed by the president of the Presidency who was also the president of the SDA, Alija Izetbegovic, dated 31 January 1993 where he was asking for the regional board to help set up the Mostar province?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it is not in keeping because we are talking about the districts and here we are talking about the implementation of a plan that came from the international community. The provinces were there in the Vance-Owen Plan and the districts were contained in the decision of the Presidency that we have had the opportunity to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you were if look at, for instance, if we look at the very last page of this letter before we get to the list of delegates, we see that it says: "As far as the ministry is informed, so far there has been no formal reply or opinion received from Mr. Mate Boban. Therefore, the Ministry of Defence again starts the initiative that the Mostar and Livno districts are put into function and it proposed to the government of RBiH that it forwards to the Presidency of RBiH in accordance with Articles 56 and 60 of the Decree Law, the draft decision." Let me ask you this -- did you find that section, sir, this is the letter dated February 25th, 1993, setting up the Mostar Livno districts and it's signed by Munib Bisic.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Munib Bisic, who is he to start with?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the assistant defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why would the Defence Ministry be asking the -- be taking the initiative in setting up the Mostar and Livno district? Keeping in mind that we also have a civilian government? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed this with Mr. Munib Bisic, but I assume that it was this other military segment, that's one thing. But another thing that I wanted to say is that I don't think that it was his job. I don't think that he should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well yesterday when we began our discussion, we looked at what Lord Owen had indicated where he had said in his book that at some point, the Muslim -- the Presidency, in fact, was a Muslim Presidency for the Muslims, and it was more or less run by his close associates. At this point in time in history, is the Presidency functioning in the manner in which it should have functioned based on the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency should have functioned on the basis of the constitution but as of the 20th December, 1992, in its own constitutive sense, the Presidency no longer functioned fully in accordance with the constitution and the same goes for the period that we are now talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in looking at the previous document which was dated January 31, 1993 you were able to tell us a little bit about what was happening at the negotiating tables with the internationals. Can you help us out a little bit, early March 1993, what is happening with the negotiating process, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in early March 1993, the negotiations on the peace agreement for Bosnia and Herzegovina based on the Vance-Owen Plan were already well underway. As I said yesterday, in March, the two sides, the Muslim and the Croat side had already signed the Vance-Owen Plan. We agreed about the provinces based on this plan, the number of those provinces and their delineation, conditionally speaking, their borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to that. Now let's look at the next document which is 1D 01972. This in binder 1, Your Honours, 1D 01972. And we don't seem to have a date, it says 1993 on it. It's addressed to Lagumdzija, as I understand, at the time, he was the vice-president of the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see at the last page, this is from Dr. Jadranko Prlic although we don't have a signature. Have you had a chance to look at this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the very first line, it talks about, it says: "In your letter without number of 3 March 1993, you informed me of the conclusions of the government ..." and so on and so forth. From reading the document, did it appear to you that this document here, 1D 01972 is in connection to the document that we've just looked at 1D 02418, that is -- I mean 1D 02565?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion as to what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is conveying here? Particularly where he talks about in paragraph 4, where he says: "The foundation of Mostar and Livno districts has not been regulated either by the current constitution or the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was signed by both the Muslims and the Croat delegations at the peace negotiations in Geneva and Washington."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Geneva and New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are absolutely right. I don't know where Washington came from. Maybe I'm still thinking of Mr. Biden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that in this document, Mr. Prlic is warning the Muslim side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in this case, it's Mr. Lagumdzija who is the prime minister, that they should comply with the international agreements, the constitution, and the laws. That they should comply with what the Muslim and Croat representatives had signed during the international negotiations and this is something that he actually was not doing at the time. And he also notes here that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is a temporary entity and that once the negotiations came into effect, it would be changed, accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But more concretely, because we can read what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is trying to convey, but can you give us a sense, from your own opinion, having been the president of the government where Dr. Jadranko Prlic is stating for instance, in the second to last paragraph: "Since your proposal is not based on the existing constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the signed constitutional principles on the future constitutional order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I do not consider it to have a legal basis or to be in keeping with the peace negotiations." I want your opinion, sir, not what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is stating, but what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think first of all that Mr. Jadranko Prlic is right when he is issuing this warning to the competent authorities that all the elements both in the constitution and in the international negotiations should be abided by as should the elements in the agreements reached by the two peoples. This letter, however, Mr. Lagumdzija's letter was sent without my knowledge and had I known about it, I would not have approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next topic. This deals with January 1993. It may appear that I'm going in and out of periods but the -- I have arranged the direct in a topical fashion, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that in the end, it will make some sense. If we look at the next document, 1D 01314. 1D 01314. That would be in the next binder so if we could have the assistance of the usher. The next binder, binder number 2. Number 1 for you, Your Honours. Have some pity on the documents, sir. Okay. 1D 01314. This is from the Security Council and it's dated 6 January 1993. First, let me ask you, were you at the negotiations in Geneva at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend negotiations in Geneva but perhaps at this time -- yes, I was at the negotiations in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you were to look at annex 1, we would see, and this is something that I will ask you to comment on, if we go to annex 1 which is on page 6. In this instance, it's on the top left-hand side, annex 1, do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see: Bosnian Croat, Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic and then Commander Milivoje Petkovic. And then we see: Bosnia and Herzegovina Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, commander in chief Sefer Halilovic, Kasim Trnka and Hajrudin Somun. And then we see that there is also a list of Bosnian Serbs, Karadzic, Mladic, Buha, Lukic, Plavsic. Sir, yesterday you talked a little bit about this, but I believe you tried to explain this concept to no avail, that is, to Senator Biden but when we look at Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what your objection was?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I objected saying that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be represented by representatives of the three peoples or a delegation that would comprise members of all three peoples. In this specific case, as you can see, we have delegations from the three parties that are taking part in the negotiations, the Croat party. The second one that is led by Izetbegovic is the Muslim party. The third one is the Serb party. And those negotiations were also attended by the delegations of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just ask this question and it may be a silly question but did you ever complain because it would appear here that at least from Bosnia and Herzegovina, we have all Muslims. And it would appear that you have the government versus two of the nations negotiating as opposed to the three nations, one of which is cloaked under the caption "Bosnia and Herzegovina" which may give it some form of legitimacy as if it is acting on behalf of the state as opposed to acting on behalf of its people.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to note here for the benefit of the Honourable Trial Chamber that before that, we had discussed this in Sarajevo at a meeting of the Presidency and that at my insistence, the Presidency agreed that abroad, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I said yesterday, can be represented by a delegation comprising members of all three peoples. And if the issue at hand was the internal organisation of the state, then the three peoples should talk to each other and they should all three have their representatives. In this specific case, regardless of the fact that I was the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was a member of the delegation of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina as is indicated here. This delegation was led by Mr. Mate Boban. I was not in the delegation headed by Alija Izetbegovic. Had we talked about Bosnia and Herzegovina's relations with some other international players, then I would be sitting there side by side with Mr. Izetbegovic and there would be a Serb representative or Serb representatives, indeed, as had been agreed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I objected in Geneva and my objection was along those lines. I demanded to have this corrected and the co-chairmen agreed with me and with the explanation that I proffered, but quite often, Alija Izetbegovic and his Muslim associates continued to be seen and recognised as the delegation, the government delegation in the international context. The delegation -- this delegation was considered to be equal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could confirm this by the fact that the three parties signed this agreement. That was an agreement, an internal agreement between the three of them. It was not signed by one representative on behalf of everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very quickly here, under Bosnia and Herzegovina we know what Alija Izetbegovic is we know Haris Silajdzic, we know Halilovic. Kasim Trnka, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kasim Trnka was a judge of the Constitutional Court for a while, I cannot confirm and remember whether he was a judge of the Constitutional Court at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the other gentleman, Somun?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Somun worked in the BH Presidency as an advisor and later on he was appointed ambassador to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So of those listed -- and I know this is purely for the record but of those listed under Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is five of them, how many nations are been represented?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All five people are Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would like to remain for a moment with this situation and be clear of what you have in mind, sir. These were negotiations mainly between the constituent narod of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they were three. Now, you complain that the Muslim section appears here under the title of "Bosnia and Herzegovina," and I can accept that. Formally, it makes sense. But if one looks at the substance, would one not have to say that there ought to have been four delegations, namely one of each narod and one which would have been sort of a father or parent delegation that would have represented Bosnia and Herzegovina as a tripartite entity? Now, would that -- is that a realistic -- is that a realistic proposition? Do you -- could you imagine how this would have looked in Geneva? How this could have been brought about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say here what was discussed and what was concluded at a meeting of the Presidency, and means that the three peoples or rather the representatives of the three peoples would conduct internal talks, they would talk to each other, and then after that, the Presidency as a whole, the Presidency which also consisted or should have consisted of representatives of several peoples would adopt those documents if they were fit to be adopted or if they were acceptable. So the first remark I want to say is that representatives of only one people were put under the header of "Bosnia and Herzegovina." That could have been considered a formal issue but given the war, it became a substantive issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not know if it was the end of the answer. Is it the end your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the end of my answer. I hope it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It does not exactly respond to my question, but I will leave it at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me pick up on this a little bit, Mr. Akmadzic. First of all, you said that this could have been a formal issue but then it turned out to be a substantive issue. You say that on page 44, I believe it's line 9 and 10 and 11. What do you mean by a substantive issue? No, no, it's not in the document. Mr. Akmadzic. Mr. Akmadzic, please listen to my question. I'll direct you to a page. I was referring to the transcript here. You indicated that the Muslim party being put under the banner of Bosnia and Herzegovina could have been a formal issue, but it turned out to be a substantive issue. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that, I meant that if it were just a technical error, then it's a formal issue, a technical issue. But if we take into account that we're talking about three constituent people with equal status and that this kept on cropping up, this was not the only instance, then it became a substantive issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back to a question that was asked of you and I would ask you to please answer it directly. And the question that was posed that, okay, you have three different nations so you can have three different parties, each nation would have its representatives but then perhaps there should be a fourth group that would represent the state itself. So would that have been better, number one? And number two, would it have been possible under the circumstances as they existed back then? And I believe I caught the essence of the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the end result would be the same. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprises two plus two plus two plus one members, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not reach an agreement on vital issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina because the Serb side wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here and kindly listen to my question. The question was: Was it possible, under the circumstances back then, for the Presidency, acting on behalf of the state, to have a delegation there? So you would have a Muslim delegation, a Croat delegation, a Serb delegation, and a BH delegation? Was it possible under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could -- there was an issue as far as that being, perhaps, the parent delegation. Well what about the international community, could that have been seen as sort of a parent delegation with the three constituent parties doing the negotiating? Or was that what the international community was doing, acting as the parent delegation, sort of trying to get the three parties to sit in a room and hammer out an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no talk of a solution like that, introduce a fourth party. Nobody mentioned this at the negotiations. Talking of the parent delegation, in the sense of someone coordinating between the various parties, and those would have been the chairmen not the peace conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'll go along the question put by counsel and also the question put by my colleague, my fellow Judge. So there was this conference in Geneva with the three constituent peoples, Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims. They each can have their own delegation, that's one thing.
