However, as was pointed out by my fellow Judge, could it not be envisaged also to have a fourth delegation which could have been the Presidency of BH itself being made up of representatives of each nation together with the then prime minister and possibly a couple more personalities. So you would have had four components, all this being conducted by the then president, Mr. Izetbegovic. Was that sort of thing not possible? If it was not possible, why was it not? Because you were part of it. You were inside it. We were -- we are outside. We can't be in the know of things but you can. And we know, though, how things work. Was it possible, doable, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must point out that the talks were organized by the cochair men, Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance. The talks of the three peoples were something that they proposed and they had our agreement for this; however, the honourable Trial Chamber is asking a question here and I think the response might be the following: Often, not this time in Geneva however, but otherwise the Presidency had its own meetings that that ran parallel to the talks that were in progress. One could say on the one hand you had three delegations having talks under the leadership of the co-chairmen and on the other hand, there was an extended Presidency normally not including any military representatives because they had their own separate talks and they were discussing similar issues, both domestically and abroad. Therefore, the Presidency did not have its own delegation. Rather, it travelled in it's entirety to these talks and held these talks. They talked, for example, to the European Union delegation in Brussels and this was done at their own initiative whenever the Presidency so decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas. I hope this -- my question was not an obstacle on your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, but let me just ask one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday -- yesterday, you said at some point that Izetbegovic would meet privately with his associates and would act as if he were the head of the state as opposed to first among equals in this collective body called the Presidency. My question is: Given the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic was first the head of his own party, the president of the SDA, and given the way he was acting and behaving, in closed doors with his associates, and promoting himself as the head of a state, how possible would it have been to put together a credible, viable, realistic, trustworthy delegation from the Presidency that would act as an honest broker on behalf of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't possible in practical terms. I suppose this was also the reason why this never came to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my characterisation and the way Mr. Izetbegovic was behaving, was that correct or incorrect at this point in time, in other words, in the history of the Presidency while you were serving there? We're talking January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Even when decisions were passed by the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic would run counter to this and do something else. I'm not saying that this was the case every single time, but it was known to have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think this was a rather crucial moment, these talks in Geneva, and it is an important issue. Mr. Akmadzic, you were also there. Did Izetbegovic in these negotiations claim and/or acquire a special status because of his formal position as president of the Presidency or president of the War Presidency, whatever? Or was he dealt with like the Croat or the Serb delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The co-chairmen who were in charge of these negotiations were very fair in the way they controlled the negotiations. However, in a purely ceremonial sense, President Izetbegovic took precedence over other people in terms of accommodation, in terms of seating arrangements during the talks. Regardless of this as the thee delegations, I think we all had the same treatment during the actual talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, admittedly for somebody who is a lay person or who is not from your country, it is very hard to understand the concept of Presidency. Indeed, in western democracies, the Presidency is always embodied by the head of state. But listening to you, one does understand that for you, this Presidency or Mr. Izetbegovic did not have the mandate to negotiate on his own, because he was a part of the Presidency and that there were at least three components, and it was not up to him to decide for everybody. But if I put myself in the shoes of the negotiators, Lord Owen or others, did they understand that well, as far as you could see? Did they understand that in fact, Mr. Izetbegovic was one among others and not the head of state as that position is understood in England and France or Germany? Could it be that there was a confusion that you may have perceived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Lord Owen and Mr. Cyrus Vance understood our situation. They gained an understanding of the situation through ongoing negotiations. They were deeply involved in the talks and they knew about everything both good and bad that was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They travelled to Sarajevo as well as other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They realised how complex the entire situation was regardless of the fact that in their own countries, the state apparatus was very much unlike the one in Bosnia. You have a country with three constituent people such as Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this country produces, in a way, this complex situation where you have a head of state like that, a collective head of state where everyone is represented. There is even a slot or a position in that collective body that belonged to the so-called "others" in other words not one of the three major groups. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan takes into account this group defined as "others" in any situation where this was an open possibility. When I say "others" I mean those not declaring themselves as Croats, Muslims, or Serbs. There are various ethnicities in Bosnia, Montenegrins, Jews, Yugoslavs, who remained, as we say, non-declared and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to move along. I hope my follow-up questions were not counted against me. P 01158. I just thought I'd throw that in, try it sneak it in, you know. Binder number 4, Your Honours. P 01158. This is a -- we've seen this before, this is a presidential transcript dated 15 January 1993 and quite clearly, if we look at the bottom in English, that is, on the right-hand corner on page 40, for instance, we see your name so we know -- it would appear, at least, that you were present at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't want to go into too much into this because we don't have time but can you -- does everybody have it? Okay. If you could tell us by and large what the nature of the conversation was on this particular occasion 15 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that we were just back from Geneva. We concluded that the talks in Geneva were crucial; however, equally crucial would be the New York talks. In this specific instance, President Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia, had just invited us for talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just very briefly, if we look at see what you're saying on page 40, you say: "Thank you for allowing me to express an opinion. Namely as far as the functioning of the government in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, I think the situation in the state administration is worse for the Croats than the situation for the Muslims in Mostar mentioned by Mr. Izetbegovic." "I will give you just a few facts." "In the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think there are 15 posts for senior government posts. Only one Croat has been taken on board since the latest elections, apart from me as the Secretary-General and he would have been dismissed if it hadn't been for my intervention. The situation is similar in the government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the assembly. Several of our people have been dismissed, relieved of their duties for unknown reasons." "I really must say that in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the government in which we talk about relations parity, the Croats have a very symbolic role." "I would add that it seems to me, and I think it is true, but I do not want to say it's 100 per cent, that the Croats, with the approval by the Croatian Democratic Union have so far appointed only one diplomat, and it's the lady who does the organisation for us in the embassy in Zagreb who organises this meeting. Many people have been appointed without consultation with us and without the knowledge of the Croatian Democratic Union ..." et cetera. I want to pick up on something else. I think that the whole problem of relations lies in this. Then further down you say - I'll skip a couple paragraphs - you say: "Then I think you must urgently start implementing what has been proposed today to form a new government that would function according to a legal principle, a principle of agreement where all three peoples will participate or take part." Now, let's see what Mr. Izetbegovic says. He says, "I cannot tell you now how much of this is right or how much is not. I think precisely because there are a number of facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. This is on page 42. He says: "I think precisely because there are a number of facts, it would be good if you could help us, as I said, to start up a body to help us in this transitional period until all of this, until all of this is established altogether."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, sir, is this: How is it possible that Alija Izetbegovic would not know that he doesn't have Croats in the government when you were able to tell us -- to tell him at the time? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible. Mr. Izetbegovic paid little attention to what I was saying about the ethnic breakdown in relation to those positions. He was talking about other things and his general modus operandi was to simply to postpone things whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You missed -- the essence of my question was this: You said that there are 15 posts for even senior government posts, and there's only one Croat. Is it possible that Izetbegovic would not have known that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was aware of the fact, and he was about to dismiss that particular Croat. He didn't on account my intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So the next part -- his answer is: "It would be good if you could help us set up a body in this transitional period." Now, you were asking for action to be taken. Concretely, was it necessary to set up a -- to have the internationals, Lord Owen, and Cyrus Vance help to set up a body to make appointments? Was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't. We could have done this ourselves. Regardless, Mr. Izetbegovic was not willing to take that course of action. His statement was just in order to leave President Tudjman was the impression that he was willing rather than to actually do anything specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go on to the next document, 1D 01512 [sic], 1512. That's in binder 1. Binder 1. Do you have the document, sir? 1D 01512.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 21, that's right. You're absolutely right. That's what I meant to say. 1521, I apologise to everybody, I -- Now, if we look at the original version, on the second page, we see it's Mostar and it seems to have a date, January 18, 1993. I want you to look at the signatures because one of them, there seems to be your name and there's a signature below it and then there is some handwriting where it says Boban underneath that. Under your name, whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine. And Mr. Boban signed the letter and the PS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please explain to us what this letter is about?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this letter, we are warning Mr. Izetbegovic that we should deal with our mutual problems without going to the Security Council. We were always saying that we were partners, friends, and that we wanted cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But with respect to a decision that had been issued on January 15th by the executive authority in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna dealing with the issue of subordination that's been characterized as an ultimatum, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please explain to us, given that you were in Geneva and given that you were in Zagreb, what was your understanding at the time? Because afterwards, you send this letter as well.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in Geneva we, to all practical intents, agreed a peace plan. As I said yesterday, all the parties accepted the principles along which Bosnia and Herzegovina would be organised. We agreed on the provinces, we reached a military agreement which defined how exactly the military forces would withdraw to their open provinces. We also agreed that the plan should take effect as soon as possible because we had also agreed a cease-fire. Based on this and following a proposal by Mr. Boban, orders were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, then -- go ahead. I'm sorry. Go ahead, finish.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These orders addressed two elements: One being resubordination, the other being the establishment of a joint command. The purpose and objective of this was not resubordination itself, this was just an intermediary measure necessary in order to be able to set up a joint command. Do you want me to go on explaining this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be fine. Now if we go to the next document 1D 00820. That's in binder 1, Your Honours. This is dated 20 January 1993. And if you look at the original, it's very difficult to read but at the top, it says Intercontinental, that's a hotel in Zagreb, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom, there appears to be the name, a signature. Do you recognise the name and the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the late Mr. Boban's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think we have discussed this before so -- well, were you aware that this had been sent off?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, Boban was sharing information with me to the extent possible. In this specific case, I'm not quite sure because it was precisely on that day, the 20th of January, 1993, because of some problems that had arisen in relation to the letter that we mentioned a while ago, that Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance called me, Boras and Miro Lasic. We travelled to Sarajevo to primarily try to resolve with the Muslims the issue of the emerging clashes in Donji Vakuf. Another objective was to allay the tensions and to diffuse the situation that then came about as a result of that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very quickly if we can look at two documents. 1D 073 -- 2730, 1D 02730, binder 3. This is a letter -- this is a publication Vecernji List, call for peaceful resolution of the conflict and it seems to be "Contents of a letter sent by Mate Boban and Mile Akmadzic to Alija Izetbegovic calling for disputed matters to be discussed at a joint meeting and not before the UN Security Council." Do you recall sending this letter off, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does this publication accurately reflect what the contents of the letter were to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we look on to the next document, 1D 02729, binder 3, Your Honours. Same publication. This is dated 22 January 1993. This is an interview with Mate Boban and Mile Akmadzic. This is in Zagreb. If we look to page 2, it says, "Truce with Muslims" and here it says: "The prime minister of BH Mile Akmadzic spoke about the talks held in Sarajevo. He stated that the Muslim side had shown their true feelings about equality of nations in BH even before the talks began since they agreed to admit to the negotiations two members of the Presidency, Mr. Boras and Mr. Lasic only after an hour of hard persuasion by the Croatian side and the co- chairmen of the Geneva conference." Did that occur, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I would like an explanation why, if they are two members of the Presidency -- and you have the co-chairmen there and you're trying to resolve a situation, why Izetbegovic or the Muslim side was preventing these two gentlemen from participating in the negotiation process.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Sarajevo because we were invited by Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance. It was very difficult to organise that because we had to travel on huge cargo planes that were used to transport humanitarian relief supplies. We arrived in Sarajevo, but Mr. Izetbegovic said that he wanted to discuss those problems that had cropped up only with me, not with Mr. Boras and Mr. Lasic. I refused and I said we were all members of the Presidency and that we were all equal as such, but Mr. Izetbegovic was still reluctant because he thought that it would be easiest for him to reach an agreement with me because of our -- the nature of our relationship and Izetbegovic agreed for this joint meeting attended by everyone to be held at the insistence of the co-chairmen and in the end, the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, later on in this interview, you say -- or I'm sorry first Mr. Boban then you: "Asked if the Croats still believed that Alija Izetbegovic was the legitimate president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Boban said that he is the president of the Presidency, the first among several equal members and that in accordance with the constitution, his second mandate had ended." Is that true? Has his mandate ended by then?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already noted in this courtroom, his term of office expired on the 20th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why did he refuse to give up the position of the president of the Presidency and simply not just take a seat as one of the members?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is necessary to apprise the Trial Chamber of the following: On the 20th of December, 1991, when the first term of office expired for Mr. Izetbegovic, at the session of the Presidency it was possible to extend his term of office under the law and the rules of procedure, Fikret Abdic and two Serb representatives, Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic voted against this extension. The Croatian side could have joined them but two of our Presidency members voted in favour of Izetbegovic's term of office being extended. This, despite the fact that in accordance with the rotation system that I have already described on the basis of the ethnic background of the Presidency members, we were supposed to hold the Presidency after Mr. Izetbegovic. So Mr. Izetbegovic's term of office was extended for another year precisely because of the Croat vote. And then one year later, he could no longer remain on that position under the law and in light of our votes, and the explanation that he proffered was that the army would not allow him to step down. I asked him this, and this is what he said to me openly: We Croats had the option of leaving the Presidency or taking it and neither option was favourable for us because we wanted to keep Bosnia and Herzegovina alive and together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. As we are now talking about legitimacy of the Presidency. Another witness, sir, has raised an issue by stating that at this time, what we had in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a War Presidency and not a normal Presidency. Now, I see here again in the documents, one doesn't come upon the title War Presidency, it says Presidency all the time. In your view, does that constitute an element of illegality or is it a formality without further weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the constitution, the only body that existed at the time was the War Presidency. We often left the "war" out in order to make things simpler, this attribute. Another reason was that if the Presidency did not discuss military matters, then the prevailing opinion was that a military representative was not so important but it is true that it was a War Presidency that was set up after the state of war was declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to follow up on the question put by Judge Trechsel. Witness, on several occasions, we heard witnesses indicate that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a Presidency which was assuming the function of head of state and this constituted the Presidency and not -- it was not only the president of the Presidency but the whole Presidency. So the Presidency was supposed to be at the head of the military and not the president of the Presidency, therefore, if the mandate of the president of the Presidency had expired, I would like to ask a practical question. What was foreseen in your system to prevent usurpers to assume the functions of the Presidency knowing that the president of the Presidency was a primus inter pares, a first among equals and that he had no powers. In a nutshell, I would like to know if the military, for instance, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not act according to the principles of law instead of following some usurper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this issue will be raised again in the course of my testimony, but I would like to say at this point that the president of the Presidency did usurp power. He did consider himself to be the Supreme Commander and not the Presidency which was, in fact, the collective Supreme Commander. The BH army did react in writing, in fact, to a letter sent by Mr. Fikret Abdic. I'm referring to Mr. Delic, who went on to become the chief of the General Staff and in that letter, it is stated that Alija Izetbegovic's decisions will be complied with regardless of everything else. And this letter was disseminated in the ranks of the BH army and Mr. Fikret Abdic protested against that at the Presidency meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And I just wanted to let the Trial Chamber know that we do have those minutes of the meeting with Mr. Abdic complaining, so we will get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Akmadzic, we have about an hour and ten minutes to go today. If I could -- we're going to move to another subject, primarily dealing with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the signing of it, that is. So if we could look at 1D 02852. Binder 3, Your Honours. 1D 02582 and I'm going to ask that you keep your answers rather short, we're going to move rather quickly. Do you see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at -- we see that the date is 3 March 1993, a date that we've seen before in another case, another document. If we look at paragraph number 3, it says: "The Security Council demands that the leaders of all the parties to the conflict in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina remain fully engaged in New York in a sustained effort with the cochairmen of the steering committee of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia to reach quickly a fair and workable settlement." Sir, were you in New York at the time and did you remain there to be fully engaged as was requested by the Security Council, by the President of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if you go to the next document, 1D 02853. Binder 3, Your Honours. Again this is 3 March 1993. We see similar to a document that we saw yesterday, this is a letter from Mr. Sacirbey who is the ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the UN at the time. And it says here, "I have the honour to present to you the agreement signed on 3 March 1993 and it says Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Mate Boban, and Akmadzic." If we go to the next -- if we turn to page -- we see the annex and this is the agreement. Now, sir, in the agreement it calls for nine members of an interim Presidency but the nine members of the interim Presidency shall designate one member to serve as the president of the Presidency. Well first of all, was this agreement ever acted upon?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement was signed before the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was signed finally, and this agreement was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at paragraph number 9, it says, that: "All parties have submitted the following six names to serve on the interim Presidency, Fikret Abdic, Mile Akmadzic, Franjo Boras, Ejup Ganic, Alija Izetbegovic and Miro Lasic." And I take it the other three would have been Serb representatives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 02903, this is in binder 3, Your Honours, we actually see the agreement and if we look at the last page dated March 3, 1993 we see several signatures. Can you confirm to us that this is your signature under your name?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can confirm that for other signatures too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You read my mind. 1D 01193, that's the very next document. This is in binder 1, Your Honours. If we look at this document, it's dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, I know that time is money but please give us at least half a minute to find the document and to then react to your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wish time was money though, but I take your point. Okay. Do we all have the document? Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This -- we see here, this is dated 16 March 1993 and it says here at the very top: "The War Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina at a joint meeting held on 14 March 1993, with the participation of members of the BH government, a number of deputies in the BH Assembly from seven political parties and it lists them, a large number of religious, cultural and public figures representing the city of Sarajevo after a broad discussion about the progress and achievements of the peace negotiations on BH in Geneva and New York and bearing in mind of position taken by BH government on 11 March 1993 adopt these conclusions." My first question is: Were you involved in this deliberation where these conclusions were allegedly adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the Presidency, but I was involved in the part that pertained to New York and the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about this document, these conclusions here. Were you part of the preamble to the conclusions stated: The War Presidency and a joint meeting held on 14th of March. Did you participate at that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just let's look at the second page and see, because I find it rather curious that religious leaders, the War Presidency, members of the government, members of the political parties would state, for instance, at the very -- on 3.9, where it says: "An implementation of the programme which clearly defined the mechanisms, forces and schedule deadlines must be an integral part of the peace plan. This particularly refers to A, cease-fire; two, withdrawal of heavy weapons; and 3, withdraw of Chetnik forces from the part of the occupied territories in compliance ..." and then the following, the very last paragraph, it says: "If the Chetnik delegation does not sign the peace package in its entirety, our delegation will again submit a request to the Security Council for a partial and immediate lifting of the embargo on imposed arms of BiH." And it's signed by Izetbegovic and it's dated 14 March 1993. Now, the word Chetnik in this Chetnik delegation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, I wonder whether you would not like to give a basis for the witness to comment this document because he was not present there, he did not say that he had ever seen it. He only said that he was involved in New York so I think you're a bit in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, if I would be given enough leeway to ask a question and then if you think that the question is out of order or is not relevant or is calling for speculation or is beyond the knowledge of the witness to answer, I would gladly withdraw the question. But my question is with respect to Chetniks. It's like calling -- it's a very pejorative term, and I'm sure that the gentleman living in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time might have heard this. I mean it's like calling Croats Ustasha and I can go on and on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My point was this: Would -- if you're trying to get somebody at the negotiating table like the Serbs, do you call them Chetniks? Because we're talking about the Chetnik delegation, and this clearly demonstrates Mr. Izetbegovic's frame of mind. That's my opinion but I'm asking the gentleman, this term back then was this appropriate to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I failed -- I swore today I was not going to get on my feet. That one I just can't let go by. We don't need a witness here. Mr. Karnavas can ask the questions and give the answers at the same time. This is my opinion. And he's just -- if anyone is listening to the questions, if the Judges might intervene occasionally when the question is inappropriate, it would be helpful, and I did not want to get on my feet today, I thought I just won't say anything; but this is ridiculous. Look at the question. Mr. Karnavas himself says that's my opinion and then asks the witness if he agrees. This is totally absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By referring to the Chetnik delegation, I know you weren't there, but who are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me to speak my mind on this. The word "Chetnik" is used here. It is 100 per cent certain that this word would never have been used had I been at that meeting. This is a term of abuse. It's something about the Chetniks from World War II, given our mutual relation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the words Chetnik and Ustasha are acceptable in street talk but certainly not at meetings of the Presidency and certainly this is not something that can ever be endorsed as signed by the president of the Presidency, the supreme body of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So much about the use of the word Chetnik. Should there be any further questions about this subject, I'm perfectly willing to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tie in with what Mr. Karnavas was saying and I was thinking the same. When you find this term in a document of this type, what does that say of the person who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who signed this document is here resorting to a term of abuse to show his or her disagreement with a party. In this case, I, too agree, that there were a number of Serb paramilitary units that referred to themselves as Chetniks. Nevertheless, as I said today, each people have the right to call themselves whatever they like. It is certainly not our place to come up with a name for them or for any other group, especially not a name that they themselves would find less than acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask one more question. You saw the agreement, we saw the letter from Sacirbey. Now let's look at this conclusion. I know you weren't present but we see that under paragraph 3 it says, "The Vance-Owen Peace Plan for BH basically considered as acceptable provided the necessary amendment are made to it particularly the following ..." and my question was knowing that you weren't there, but you were there at the negotiations, you were there when the agreement was signed, were these conditions part of the agreement when the agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that what we see here is an extended Presidency meeting. Yesterday, I said that the Presidency had the right to invite anyone to one of its meetings. In this case, the number of political parties were invited, the Presidency wanted to hear them out. The Presidency wanted to hear the position of those assembly delegates who were able to come to the meeting. They wanted to hear the political parties. What follows from this is that the Presidency in its most amplified composition as a head of state, as the assembly, and as the War Presidency, accepted the Vance-Owen Plan under these conditions that we see here. When the Vance-Owen Plan was signed, President Izetbegovic submitted to the co-chairmen the conditions elaborated on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, let me just focus you on my question because I have very limited time, very, very limited time. Were these conditions part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these terms were not part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wouldn't the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, you know, Your Honour, the document, the Court has the actual peace agreement signed and put in the UN record and I think that's a far better answer what the terms of the agreement are than what this witness may recall today, and the conditions are in the document. If the Chamber reads it you will see the conditions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Setting aside the document, sir, were these conditions negotiated upon during the negotiations prior to the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were negotiated, but they weren't agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just now one question that comes up. In point 3.4, "It is here stated that the provinces should not be ethnic areas." Is that included in what you say was not part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Do you think that's in contrast with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? It's at the bottom of the page in the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. There is one thing that I would like to point out. The provinces under the Vance-Owen Plan were envisaged in such a way as to meet to the greatest extent possible the criteria that I defined yesterday. One of these was the ethnic criterion but there were others too. Despite this, the provinces would not bear ethnic names. They would be designated depending on their capital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So I don't know -- I not have yet a precise answer. This point, saying that the provinces are not ethnic areas, is that compatible with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in your view or is that something which, as you have generally said of these conditions, is not in accordance with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in keeping with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan or rather with the nine principles adopted in Geneva on the 4th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just -- this is a follow-up question to make sure because I don't want to mislead anybody or for the Trial Chamber to believe that you have misled them. Are all these conditions consistent with what was agreed at ...

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the following proviso: Mr. Izetbegovic talked about this military body, the Serb side that he describes as the Chetnik side, he submitted this on a separate sheet of paper, and it wasn't part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in Geneva, were the Serbs referred to as Chetniks, as a Chetnik delegation? Is that -- did they have a placard there, Chetnik delegation, Karadzic and what have you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as can be gleaned from all these documents, they were one of the parties to these talks, and they described themselves as the Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well I know how they would -- they described themselves but Mr. Akmadzic, and I want you to be very clear on this, were they being referred to by others, did Izetbegovic ever say, for instance: Here come the Chetniks. Glad to see, you Mr. Chetnik Karadzic, were they referred to as Chetnik, not what the Serbs referred to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a term of abuse that was sometimes used, but this is not a term that you can apply to a delegation, an official delegation so Izetbegovic never employed this term whenever the situation was formal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02885. Binder 3. Now, this is from Slobodna Dalmacija, this is on unconstitutional decisions, this is an article. Have you seen this article, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is this article referring to? Focus on number 3, paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decisions were being passed in the absence of Croatian representatives at meetings of the Presidency or other kinds of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a lone examples, these examples in fact are bounded at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, do you know whether this is in connection with the conclusion which we just saw? Because if you look at under paragraph number 3: "As announced by the Croat representatives today, they concluded at their meeting in Zagreb that 'not one representative of the Croat people who is a member of the Presidency or the government of B & H participated in the work of that session nor did any of them concent to the decisions and conclusions adopted in that session.'" Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct but in the sense of ethnic equality and not in the sense of the text that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I guess, Mr. Akmadzic, maybe it's late in the day and I don't want to spend too much time. Sir, were any Croats at that meeting to your knowledge that voted on the conclusions subsequent to the signing of the agreement any Croat members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of those Croats who were officially members of the Presidency or of the government. Maybe there were other parties that were invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We go to 1D 02908. Binder 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Your Honour, in case Mr. Karnavas wants to follow-up on it course there's been no indication of why it was those Croat members were not there. Of course the Chamber may recall previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's for cross-examination, Your Honour. That's for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just doing what Mr. Karnavas frequently does, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to see that he's picked up a few lessons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at 1D 02908. This is a report to the Secretary-General on the activities of the international conference. If we could just look at -- on page 11, you'll see page 11 on the top right-hand corner in English, and it talks about interim provincial governments, and this may assist also in answering in part the question that was asked earlier of you. Does this reflect, sir, what was being envisaged as far as the interim provincial arrangements? You see under D, interim provincial governments?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is envisaged in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go to the next document, P 02088. This is in binder 4, Your Honours. This is the joint statement. We've seen it before. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just wait for Judges to locate the document. If you look at page 3, do you recognise those signatures? In the English version, sir? Never mind. If you have the document -- sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now it says here, April 24, 1993, Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, that there was a meeting and there is a joint statement. It says here under 1, "In accordance with the agreement between Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Haris Silajdzic, Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic, concluded on March 3, 1993." Is that the agreement that we were talking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that with or without the preconditions or I should say the conditions that were -- were subsequently signed by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see here on the next paragraph, still under number one, that the coordination body will work under the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan to the extent possible. Was the coordination body ever formed for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination body was formed, but it never got off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at two very quick documents, I don't know whether you will be able to assist us, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I may come back to your first question, namely as to the signature. For my part, I do not see any signature of our witness, and I wonder whether he has an explanation as he's mentioned at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Either is for Silajdzic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at the document, sir, you see there's only signatures of Boban, Izetbegovic, Tudjman is witnessed and, of course, why is your signature not there since this is in accordance to an agreement that you and the others reached on March 3 but obviously if we look at the preamble it talks about a meeting between Izetbegovic and Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended this meeting but that didn't mean that I signed anything. This was signed by the Croat representative, by the Muslim representative, and by the witness, and that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's a small mystery here, looking at this document, but you might be able to lift it. There was a meeting on the 24th of April between Izetbegovic and Mate Boban. By the look of the document, it seems as though it had been organized by Lord Owen and Mr. Tudjman. And we find out that there are many ambassadors that are there, Okun and others. Mate Boban and Izetbegovic signed the document and all of a sudden, we see that Tudjman was there as a witness and he signed too. So I ask myself: Why didn't Lord Owen sign as well? Do you have an explanation for that? Can you shed some light on this? Why didn't he sign as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document about an agreement between the two parties. Lord Owen was a mediator. If he signed this, he may have signed it as a witness; however, at the meeting, it was agreed that both parties should sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said that he could have signed so Tudjman signed but he didn't, and this is what I fail to understand but never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if any further explanation is required, neither Lord Owen nor Cyrus Vance ever signed any this kind of document, I mean bilateral agreements not even as witnesses although the meetings were held under their aegis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the next couple of documents, we'll conclude this topic. 1D 01443, binder 1. If we look at the original version, we see a signature there. We see the name of Alija Izetbegovic. Can you confirm that that is indeed his signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Izetbegovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't have a date. We don't have a date. But -- if we look at the very first sentence, it says, "As our two sides have signed the Vance-Owen Plan, I suggest we start implementing it to the extent possible at this moment." And I underscore for the Trial Chamber to note "to the extent possible" language that was used in the agreement. And it says: "In my opinion, that would eliminate the danger of continued conflict between the army of BiH and HVO and the contribute to the restoration of the damaged confidence among the good-willed people in the free territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And in the very last sentence he says, "I am looking forward to your positive response." Before I ask you to comment on this document, I want to refer you to the next document which is 1D 02832, and that would be in binder 3, Your Honours, 1D 02832. This is dated 10 May 1993. Can you tell us whether indeed that is Mr. Boban's signature, sir? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Boban's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, it indicates, "My positive reply --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says: "My positive reply to your memorandum of 10 May 1993 in which you proposed the start of implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan to the extent to which it is possible" that phrase keeps cropping up again, "at the moment in its obligation stemming from the joint session signed on 25 April 1993." And it goes on. Mr. Boban then says in the second paragraph: "Unfortunately, the feedback information is negative because your people are not accepting it. I personally believe that you must grant the same powers to all legitimate politicians from your people because they mostly cite lack of authority when denying the offered agreements." Then he says "I also propose that you immediately set a date for a meeting of the coordinating body founded on the basis of the joint statement." You were in situ at the time. Do you know what Mr. Boban is talking about when he was replying to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban replies here that he is willing to cooperate in every way. Nevertheless, he has misgivings about whether Mr. Izetbegovic issued appropriate orders to local military and civilian authorities. If indeed he had, they were certainly not complying with them. He is again pleading with Mr. Izetbegovic to see to it that the orders were followed. Mr. Boban also wishes that the coordinating body would start operating because at this point it still wasn't. Its role was to work on behalf of the Presidency, and it had to do certain jobs under the terms of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll move on to another section. This is beginning more or less with May 1993. We see P 02254, binder 4. P 02254. This is a note by the President of the Security Council. Please look at it. We've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at -- and we're going to see a couple of documents together so I'll just read the appropriate paragraph and then move to the next document. Under paragraph number 3 says: "The Security Council strongly condemns this major military offensive launched by Bosnian Croat paramilitary units which is totally inconsistent with the signature of the peace plan for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Bosnian Croat party." Now, let's leave this document and go on to the next document, 1D 02093. 2096, I apologise, 2096, it is in binder 1. This is dated 11 May 1993. So one day later. And if we look at the very last page, we see your name and further down we see a seal and a signature. Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this letter -- did you draft this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's addressed to a Mr. Vorontsov, and he was the President of the Security Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose for drafting this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this letter was to notify the Security Council and the President of the Security Council that great difficulties had cropped up in the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan and that the BH army forces continued to attack the Croatian units and Croats, and I asked for his intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Look at paragraph number 3, you also seem to be trying to convey a message. You say, "The statement's description of the Croatian Defence Council (HVO) as 'Bosnian Croat paramilitary units' misconstrues the role of the HVO. HVO is a legitimate army recognised by the government and the Presidency ..." and it's very difficult to read the rest.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my response to an earlier document, to the document that we saw earlier where an attack by Croatian forces is being condemned, and they are being labelled paramilitaries; and I wanted to notify the President of the Security Council that those were not paramilitary Croat forces at all but a recognised element of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to ask the following: Mr. Karnavas, you also a few moments ago asked the witness to look at the document 1D 02254 which was just now referred to again by the witness and it is a Security Council document in the binder 4. That is true that in the third paragraph of that document, which was issued by the President of the Security Council, so it is not a decision of the Council but nevertheless it has significance of its own since it was issued on behalf of the Council by its President. And indeed, the third paragraph refers to Bosnian Croat paramilitary units, and it continues to say that these are attacks against the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica. Now, my question is since the -- since this letter -- this statement rather of the President was issued on the 10th of May 1993, and since we recall that the fightings in Mostar broke out, if I remember correctly, on the 9th of May then I wonder if the witness could tell us that was it a kind of outcome of the fighting which broke out in Mostar mainly, and of course in other areas as well, and what is his reaction, I mean the witness' reaction to it as far as the President's statement made on behalf of the Security Council? If it was about Mostar mainly or about other matters as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this is what we call the presidential statement. It is a very important document. As we said, this is not a resolution of the Security Council but only of the President and in this specific case, he is referring to the new developments in the situation in Mostar, the new developments from the day before, and he insists that this should stop and my -- in my response, I noted that these were not paramilitary forces; and I've already explained to you, Your Honours, that we Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina found it hard to convince the international community that we should have an equal status in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a constituent and sovereign people, that our armed forces had been recognised as such, but it was our problem that we didn't have our embassies, and we didn't have public relations. We didn't have our lobbyists and Bosnian side had all of that, the Bosnian Muslim side, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the registrar has drawn my attention to the fact that I might have misquoted the document, therefore I again I would like to say that I referred to the document 2254, 2254. That was the one which also had been mentioned by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's P 0, P 0 as opposed to 1D. It's P 0 meaning it's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, but here on that document I have already on that document 1D 02254.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since my fellow Judge spoke about this document, I would like to put a follow-up question to you. This document is dated 10th of May. You know that on the 9th May, some instance took place in Mostar. In this document, mention is also made of events that took place during the month of April 1993. The Security Council also made a statement about that. But in this particular document, mention is made of paramilitary units. You were informed about that, and we saw in that other previously shown document, you reminded that the HVO was a recognised army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the Security Council mentions problem related to military actions or actions by paramilitary units but isn't there a problem here? In response to the President of the Security Council, did you think that your letter was enough? And I have in mind document 1D 02096.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no Croat, and when I say Croat, I mean the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croat forces apart from the Croatian Defence Council. These were the Bosnian Croat paramilitary units. It's a reference to the Croatian Defence Council and my protest, if I may call it that, had to do with the fact that our armed forces, the Croatian Defence Council, were recognised, were legal. They were not paramilitary forces. The second point, in accordance with the reports that I had received from the ground, the Croatian Defence Council had not initiated military operations in Mostar on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification because on line -- on page 80, line 20, I believe, it says, "those were the Bosnian Croat paramilitary units" and my colleague tells me that she heard you say "those words." Which of the two did you say? That they were or you were referring to the quote "those words."

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that as a quote, and I said it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you did indicate as a follow-up to the questions raised by the Judges, you indicated that there was no lobby or public relations, and it's rather curious that here it is May 10th and the incident happened on May 9th, a day earlier and now you have the President of the Security Council issuing this -- this note calling the HVO Bosnian Croat paramilitary units and more or less fixing blame on one side of the conflict. To your knowledge, do you know whether the Security Council did any investigation within that 24-hour period or less to find out what had occurred and as a result they were drafting this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I move to strike from the record Mr. Karnavas's comments on page 81, line 10 through 16. I will just start doing this because nothing seems to stop Mr. Karnavas from continuing making these characterizations, arguments, and so whenever he does it I'll just stand up and ask for it to be stricken from the record that's just nothing but argument from Mr. Karnavas. The Chamber should stop it but if the Chamber doesn't then I will ask that it be stricken from the record every time it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, because I'm holding my powder dry. The gentleman indicated in his own words to a question posed by Judge Prandler, I believe that they didn't have a lobby for public relations. That is a fact in evidence now. The technique is called looping. I'm entitled to use those facts as part of my next question. Secondly, we see May 10th, Mr. President, you indicated the incident that occurred on May 9th. These again are facts in evidence, facts that were put to the witness. So when you look at my question, those lines that supposedly he wishes to strike which you cannot strike from this record, it's an impossibility, but be that as it may, these are already predicates that came out from the words of the witness or from the -- Your Honours based on previous testimony. They are facts in evidence. So this is the prelude to my question and I'm asking how is it a day later that they come up with this? What if anything does he know about a report or an investigation? Perfectly legit and I don't see anything wrong with that question. I'm really puzzled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well it's very clear, Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas can call the technique whatever he wants, he can call it looping or he can call it loopy; but the fact of the matter is he said, Isn't it curious, as an example he goes on to say, Isn't it curious, now we've lost it off the page in real time, but isn't it curious and all this commentary it's rather curious that here it is, May 10th, et cetera, et cetera, there's no reason for this. And you simply put a question. As I said yesterday and as I'll just keep saying I guess until I get tired of saying it, you ask the witness questions open-ended questions, you don't engage in commentary, you don't argue your case, you just ask open-ended questions and it's not necessary for Mr. Karnavas to continuously argue his case and characterise the evidence. It's not proper and the Chamber should stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the word curious is offensive, I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it possible, how is it possible that within less than 24 hours the President of the Security Council would be issuing this note with these characterizations and these findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does the witness have any foundation for how the witness knows how the President of the Security Council issued this within 24 hours? What is the foundation for this witness being able to answer this that question? Which again is part of the problem. It calls for pure speculation. Mr. Karnavas, it's gone on long enough today, should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go about it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether UNPROFOR or ECMM observers in situ that were able to, the degree of certainty, scientific certainty determine who was responsible, who initiated the aggression, who was involved and which forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where does the word scientific certainty come into it? Where is that a requirement anywhere? The Chamber knows the evidence. The Chamber's heard from the international observers who were there on the ground on the day in question including the Spanish battalion, so it isn't necessary for Mr. Karnavas to again argue his case instead of just simply putting fair questions to the witness. This witness has, there's no knowledge, has indicated no knowledge of any of these matters. He wasn't in Mostar. Whether he knows anything about it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I find it -- I must say, it troubles me that the members of the Bench are not putting a stop to this sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. I disagree with what Mr. Scott said but on the other hand, he is right in saying that you used the word "curious" and then you withdrew it afterwards. You started putting the question again, Mr. Scott intervened once again. He asked what the foundations were for this question. Did the witness know what happened on the 9th of May? Well, you could have asked the witness whether he knew when sending his letter to the President of the Security Council what had happened in Mostar on the 9th of May. Maybe that's what was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're probably right, Mr. President. Unfortunately, I'm dealing with a time issue. I'll move on. 1D 02728. This is a letter dated -- this is in binder 3. This is a -- dated 13 May 1993 and it says "Content of a letter sent by BH prime minister Mile Akmadzic to the UN Security Council denouncing what he considers to be an erroneous portrayal of the Croatian side in the Muslim-Croat conflict in Bosnia." Sir, you have the original version or copy it. Does this accurately reflect what you sent and what was eventually published in this particular publication?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said and this is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to the next topic. This is dealing with Medjugorje. And very quickly, we know that there was an agreement that was reached on 18 May 1993. There's no mystery by now. If you could look at 1D 02404, binder 2. First of all, were you present in Medjugorje when this agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at the bottom of the first page of 1D 02404, it talks about coordinating bodies or coordinating body. We see your name. It says, "It has been confirmed that the following persons shall make up the coordinating body as agreed in Zagreb." Yet one more agreement. Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic, Franjo Boras, Alija Izetbegovic, Ejup Ganic, Fikret Abdic, and then we see that there is a central government on paragraph Roman numeral 5 where you are featured there and then further down it says it has been agreed that Mr. Prlic shall be the prime minister. Now, I'm more interested in the coordinating body. Did it ever meet, did it ever act on the agreement, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, on the 18th of May, 1993, when, as it's indicated here, an agreement was reached in Medjugorje and this meeting was attended by all the major figures, the co-chairmen, President Tudjman, the Croat and the Bosniak party and issues discussed were the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan and other issues that were of importance at the time including the conflict that had broken out on the 9th of May in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. My question was very brief. Did the coordinating body meet as such and did it do anything that it was supposed to do based on the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination body never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to skip a few documents, and I'm going to go to 1D 02037. I'm going to ask Your Honours to keep that agreement in mind, 18th of May, 1993 in mind. This is 1D 02037, binder 1. This is from Lord Owen's book. Very quickly, this is -- if we look at what is page 196, the second to last paragraph, it says -- it's 186, it says, and I'll read slowly: "A crucial factor in my decision was Douglas Hurd's insistence on sends his deputy Douglas Hogg out to spend two and a half hours with me over lunch in Geneva on 26 May. He was accompanied by Jeremy Greenstock of the foreign office." And then it goes on. Then if we go to the next page, it says here towards the middle of the -- or the first part of the right-hand side, it says: "Douglas Hogg wanted me to admit that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was dead. I concede that had it could only be carried forward by Europe ready to take a full burden of military implementation without the US but with the eastern Europeans." My first question is, sir, did you know at that time, May 26th, as of that date, that certain European powers such as England, the UK, were trying to get Mr. Owen to concede that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was dead? And I'm asking you while you are undergoing all these efforts to implement this plan, were you made aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. It was only later that Lord Owen told me in a conversation in Geneva when I insisted on the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, he told me: Mr. Akmadzic, the Vance-Owen Plan is dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to the next document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to go to the next document and we will end with this. 1D 02914. Binder 4, Your Honours. 1D 02914. If you could look at it, please. This is from a book by Boutros Boutros-Ghali, "Unvanquished, a US-UN Saga." Now, you are familiar with this book, are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's flip to page 68, the last part of the paragraph. I will begin reading and go on to the next page: "As a presidential candidate, Clinton had called for multilateral military action in Bosnia and entered office declaring Bosnia to be America's most urgent international crisis. But the new US administration quickly threw up barriers against effective action. Cyrus Vance felt certain that the United States would accept the peace plan that he and Owen had negotiated." I'll skip a few lines. He then goes on, "The new Clinton team seemed to want to have little to do with him" meaning Vance, "and even less to do with David Owen." "Worse, the chances of peace were being thrown away, as Clinton and Christopher, using strong language, attacked the Vance-Owen Plan as appeasement of the Serbs. They were wrong. The plan delineated a ten-province structure that would reflect all groups fairly, reconstituting Bosnia as a multi-ethnic and progressively demilitarized state." I'll skip a few lines. "All this effort was tossed aside Clinton and Christopher who declared that the United States would come up with its own peace plan. They called for lifting the embargo on arms for Bosnia. They said they wanted air strikes against the Serbs, though they knew that France, Britton and Russia would not agree. An end to the arms embargo would not 'level the playing field ' to the benefit of the Muslims as the United States claimed it would; instead, as Owen said, it would create a 'killing field.'" I will skip a few lines towards the end of the page. "Vance and Owen came to my office on February 2, 1993. The previous evening, Vance had met with Christopher to brief him on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Though the EC had just announced its full and unequivocal support for the plan, Christopher seemed skeptical and negative. The Serbs had agreed to it, but the Bosnian Muslims were the holdouts largely because the negative attitude of the incoming Clinton team had convinced them that the United States would give them a better deal." I'll skip a few lines. It says then: "I decided to issue a report to the Security Council immediately urging acceptance of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. On February 8, Vance, Owen and I met with Bosnian Croat leader Mile Akmadzic prime minister of Bosnia. 'In my opinion' he said 'and that of the most citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Vance-Owen Plan is the best; there is no alternative to it but war. In our view, we cannot finish a war successfully, and victory for any side is not in prospect.' But in Washington, Bosnian Foreign Minister Haris Silajdzic was not encouraged to accept the plan US opposition had dealt the Vance-Owen Plan a severe setback, if not a death blow." Then I won't go on. Mr. Akmadzic, did you have this conversation with Boutros Boutros-Ghali as he recalls and did you state those words that he has -- that he attributes to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember when I was received by Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the co-chairmen were present, that was on the 8th February 1993 in the UN palace. On that occasion, I was introduced to -- or rather I told Boutros Boutros-Ghali together to the co-chairmen about the developments in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I said for the most part the words that you can read here, and I would stand by most of what I said on that occasion even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me conclude by asking this. It says here, this is on page 71: "Asked to explain what the United States intended, former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger said that he thought the United States wanted to reduce the 43 per cent of the territory that the Vance-Owen Plan gave the Serbs. It would take two and a half more years of bloody war and war crimes before the United States at Dayton would give the Serbs 49 per cent. David Owen later declared that if 'if George Bush had won the American elections then the war in Bosnia would have been over long ago.'" Is that a correct assessment given what was being negotiated at the Vance-Owen Peace Plan or was being envisaged and what ultimately ended up ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I object to this. How can this witness possibly answer that question whether this was an assessment by Boutros Boutros-Ghali or President Clinton or Joseph Biden. I mean this is absurd, and the question is objectionable, it should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very clear that at Dayton there were maps and there was sophisticated mechanisms in order to make sure with precision how much of the territory would be given to each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then Mr. Karnavas can present the maps then that's a better record than what this witness knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman was at the -- negotiated at the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. He was also as we heard involved throughout this process. Clearly he would be able to tell us whether the Vance-Owen Peace Plan provided more or less land to, say, the Muslims and the Croats versus what they ultimately got at Dayton and as far as the two and a half more years of fighting and the thousands of deaths, I think anyone who visits Bosnia can visit the grave yards. They'll see that. So sir could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be a question calling for speculation but can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honours. I would like to make the following statement here: There was the Cutileiro Plan that was accepted by Croats and Serbs, but was rejected by the Muslims. There was the Vance-Owen Plan that was accepted by Muslims and Croats and then rejected by Serbs then accepted by Serbs and rejected by Serbs. There was the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that was accepted by Serbs and Croats and rejected by Muslims. There was the Washington Plan that was signed by Croat and Muslims and it follows from what I've just said that Croats accepted all the plans because what they cared about was peace. There was the Dayton Agreement that the Croats signed albeit under pressure and since you are asking me for my assessment, my assessment is that it will result in a lot of problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina because many Croats will move out since they are not accorded the status of an equal -- of the equal people because many Croats were killed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 2 per cent of all the Croats were wounded in the war and that's a very high percentage. But at any rate, this assessment here stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there might be a technical problem but that will be settled tomorrow. My apologies to the interpreters. We are nearly 7 minutes past the usual time. We'll try to make it better next time. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15. Unless I'm mistaken you must have some 45 minutes left, Mr. Karnavas. So count on three-quarters of an hour tomorrow, and then we'll have the other counsel. Thank you, see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
